analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $20 an hour, ends subminimum wages for tipped workers, teens, and workers with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $20 an hour over three years and phase out the subminimum wages for tipped workers, new teen hires, and workers with disabilities, but it has only been referred to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill raises the federal minimum wage in steps from $7.25 to $10, then $13, $16.50, and $20 an hour over three years. After that, the wage rises automatically each year by the greater of inflation or GDP growth. It also eliminates the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped workers over six years, and phases out the wages below the minimum that employers are allowed to pay some teenagers and some workers with disabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage — disproportionately adults in their prime working years in restaurants, retail, care work, and other low-paid service jobs — would see raises in steps up to $20 an hour. Tipped workers would eventually be guaranteed the full minimum wage plus their tips, and employees with disabilities who are currently paid special subminimum wages under federal certificates would be moved to the full minimum within six years. Workers in states where the state minimum is lower than the new federal floor gain the most; workers in states that already require more would not be affected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers, tipped workers, disabled workers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in four steps to $20 an hour within three years of enactment — from $10 to $13 to $16.50 to $20 — replacing the $7.25 floor that has been in place since 2009.
After reaching $20, the wage is adjusted automatically every year by the greater of the Consumer Price Index or GDP growth, so it does not erode and does not depend on Congress acting again.

Phases out the tipped minimum wage over six years, so tipped workers' cash wage climbs from $6 to $20 an hour, they gain an explicit legal right to keep all their tips, and after that they must be paid the full minimum wage with tips on top.

Raises and then repeals the youth subminimum wage — the provision allowing employers to pay newly hired workers under 20 less than the minimum — starting at $6 an hour and reaching the full minimum within a few years.

Phases out federal special certificates that allow employers to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage: the required rate climbs from $5 to the full minimum over six years, no new certificates may be issued, and the whole program sunsets, while the Labor Secretary must offer transition help and referrals to competitive employment.
Adds penalties to the Fair Labor Standards Act covering tips that are 'unlawfully kept or used' by employers, strengthening enforcement against tip theft.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum or near-minimum wages — restaurants, fast food, retail, hotels, agriculture, home and residential care, and other labor-intensive service businesses — would bear higher payroll costs in steps up to $20 an hour. Small independent businesses with thin margins would feel this most and would face pressure to raise prices, trim hours, automate, or absorb lower profits. Consumers would pay some of the increase through higher prices for restaurants and other services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Indexing the wage to the greater of inflation or GDP growth is unusual and aggressive: GDP grows faster than prices in most years, so the minimum wage would keep rising well above cost-of-living levels indefinitely, embedding a real-terms increase every year rather than merely holding the $20 floor steady.

The step up to $20 an hour — nearly triple the current $7.25 federal floor — would substantially raise labor costs for restaurants, retail, agriculture, and care providers, and good-faith opponents and most economic analyses of large fast increases project some job losses or reduced hours among the very lowest-wage workers, alongside price increases.

Phasing out section 14(c) subminimum certificates ends a program some disability service providers rely on; providers have long argued that without it, some workers with significant disabilities could lose workshop-based employment options, which is why the bill includes a six-year transition and Labor Department assistance rather than immediate repeal.

Small businesses would face compliance costs from the stepped schedules — a separate four-to-six-year timeline for tipped workers, another for teen hires, another for 14(c) workers — and mandatory Federal Register notices before each increase, all while planning around a wage that changes every year afterward.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: a near-tripling of the federal wage floor, plus the end of every legal subminimum wage, reaching millions of workers whose pay has stagnated since 2009. The costs are real but narrower: higher labor bills for low-wage employers, some price increases passed to consumers, and — in most economic estimates of fast increases — a fraction of the lowest-paid workers losing hours or jobs as businesses adjust. The design question is not whether to raise the wage but how far and how fast: $20 in three years is at the aggressive end of proposals, and the GDP-plus-inflation indexation guarantees perpetual real increases rather than holding a level. The disability certificate phase-out is the part with the most credible tradeoff, though the bill's six-year runway and transition assistance are designed to address it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no further action so far in the current Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Donald Norcross of New Jersey introduced the Give America a Raise Act on February 10, 2026.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is the committee with jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act and minimum wage law.
Five House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did.
Since the referral, no further action has been recorded: no committee markup, no vote, and no floor schedule entry.
The Congress runs until January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive while it waits in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: low-wage employers keep paying the current $7.25 federal floor and the existing subminimum wages, and the bill's beneficiaries have gained nothing because it has not moved. Whether workers eventually benefit depends on the bill getting committee and floor votes before the Congress ends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; bill is stalled in committee

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set out a $20 minimum wage with full elimination of the tipped, youth, and disability subminimum wages.

for.name: Five House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Republican-controlled in the 119th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further action on it — no hearing or markup scheduled.

against.name: Restaurant, retail, and small-business lobbies
against.what_they_did: Industry groups that consistently oppose large federal minimum wage increases and the elimination of the tipped wage typically lobby committee members against bills like this one.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred; the only signal is partisan sponsorship — the sponsor and all five cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support on record.

industries.note: The most affected industry: the bill raises its base wage toward $20 an hour and phases out the tipped minimum wage entirely over six years, requiring tipped staff to be paid the full floor with tips on top. Menu prices, tip pooling disputes, and staffing levels in restaurants would all be directly reshaped.

industries.industry: Retail, hotels, and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Businesses built on minimum-wage labor would face payroll costs rising in steps to $20 an hour plus an automatic annual escalator afterward. Their workers are exactly the people the bill is designed to help, so the industry's cost is the public's gain in this bill.

industries.industry: Disability service providers holding section 14(c) certificates
industries.note: Sheltered workshops and providers that legally pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage would see required rates climb to the full minimum and their certificate authority expire after six years, with no new certificates allowed. Providers have historically argued the phase-out threatens program viability; the workers being underpaid are the intended beneficiaries.
The youth subminimum wage — currently $4.25 an hour for new hires under 20 — would rise and then be repealed, ending a discount employers could use for teenage entry-level staff.

analysis.trajectory: With only the sponsor and five cosponsors, no Republican support on record, and no committee action months after referral, the likeliest path is that the bill stays in the Education and Workforce Committee and dies when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, without a vote — the fate of most stand-alone minimum wage bills in a chamber controlled by the other party. Its main realistic route to movement would be as part of a larger package, which no source shows is happening.
